title: Your evening routine
hook: Kavi gives King Nimi one line to end the day; offer everything, then build the evening routine
carry: hand the whole day back to god

segments.voice: Yesterday, surya, the sun: Rama prayed to him on a battlefield. Your line was the sun is the god you can see.
screen: `SUNSET WITHOUT OBJECTS — THE SUN IS THE GOD YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: A king named Nimi is in the middle of a grand ceremony when nine wanderers walk in, brothers, bright as the sun, carrying nothing. Nimi stops everything, stands, and welcomes them with honor. Then he asks the question he's actually been carrying all his life: what is the best thing a person can do? The first brother, Kavi, answers, and the heart of his answer isn't a long ritual or a hard vow. It's one sentence, the kind you could say at the end of any day.
screen: `A KING, NINE WANDERERS.` → `WHAT'S THE BEST THING TO DO?` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Bhagavata Purana, and Kavi's sentence is still said in many Hindu homes, often at the close of puja or before sleep. In plain English it goes something like this: whatever I do, with my body, my words, my mind, my senses, my understanding, or simply out of my own nature, I offer it all to Narayana, to God. That's it. Not only the good things. Whatever I did. This is samarpana: offering, handing over. Krishna says much the same to Arjuna. The morning puja offers the day before it starts. The evening hands it back once it's done: the good, the hard, the moment you'd rather forget. You don't have to carry it into sleep, because it isn't only yours anymore. This week has given you the pieces. Put them together and you have an evening routine, about five minutes. First, the bell: one ring, followed all the way to silence. Second, the breath: in for four, out for six, a few rounds. Third, arti: circle a flame and take the light, or if there's no flame, face the window where the sun went down. And fourth, the offering: Kavi's line, in your own words, then Om shanti, shanti, shanti. This week an elephant, a poor friend, a meat-seller and a prince all ended up in the same place: handing something over to God. Tonight, it's your turn.
screen: `WHATEVER I DO, I OFFER IT.` · `SAMARPANA: HANDING IT OVER.` · `BELL, BREATH, ARTI, OFFERING.` · `OM SHANTI, SHANTI, SHANTI.`

segments.voice: Ring your bell or tap a glass and follow the sound to silence, then breathe in for four and out for six, three times. If you have a flame, circle it slowly and take the light to your eyes; if not, turn toward the window. Then name one thing from today, the best or the hardest, and offer it, in Kavi's words or your own: whatever I did today, I offer it. If you don't pray, simply set it down. Then, quietly, if you'd like: Om shanti, shanti, shanti.
Dinacharya, the course of the day: bell, breath, arti and an offering, five minutes that hand the day back instead of letting it just stop. Today's word.
Your line: hand the whole day back to God. Whatever I did today, I offer it. That's the week, and day one hundred twenty-four.

screen: `HAND THE WHOLE DAY BACK TO GOD.` → `DAY 124 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BODY AS TEMPLE.`

howItsDone: Many Hindu households close the day with evening arti at the home shrine, and many close their prayers with a verse offering all one's actions to God (kayena vacha…, from the Bhagavata Purana) and Om shanti shanti shanti.

original.note: Sanskrit dinacaryā: the daily routine, the course of the day from waking to sleep.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bedtime ritual.
what it means: handing the whole day back to God, good and bad, with a bell, a breath, a flame and one line of offering.
what a scholar hears: Kavi's verse (kayena vacha manasendriyair va, Bhagavata Purana 11.2.36) is widely recited at the close of worship; dinacharya, the daily routine, is a classical Ayurvedic idea.
